text: Designing for data freshness SLAs — turning "near real-time" into an actual number a pipeline can be measured against.

"Near real-time" is marketing language. A real freshness SLA is checkable: data is never more than N minutes older than the event that produced it. That's a non-functional requirement, and like any non-functional requirement, it's worthless until it's a number.

The batch, streaming, or hybrid choice from Lesson 5 caps what's even achievable before any pipeline code exists. Nightly batch means hours of staleness. True event streaming means seconds. You can't promise a five-minute SLA on top of a nightly job.

Lower latency generally means compute running continuously instead of spinning up once a night. The real question isn't how fresh you can make something — it's how fresh this specific consumer needs it, and whether anyone's willing to pay for that.
Freshness is measured as event time to available time, and watermarks decide how long to wait for late data. Next up: the CAP theorem, for data engineers.
